title: Raga Gond
hook: a raga where a weaver, a cloth printer and a leatherworker sing beside the Gurus

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bilaval, the hot wind passing and the thanks sung after, and your line was joy and shelter. Whom did you tell what you're glad got through? Day one thousand ninety-eight.

A weaver. A cloth printer. A leatherworker. That's how tradition remembers Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas: by their work, in a world where, tradition says, such work kept people far from the front of the temple. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to today's raga, the one that comes after Bilaval. Their hymns are there, under the same heading as the Gurus', sung to the same raga, bowed to in the same book. Today: Raga Gond.
screen: `A WEAVER, A PRINTER, A LEATHERWORKER.` → `REMEMBERED BY THEIR WORK.` → `THE SAME HEADING AS THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: Gond follows Bilaval in the Granth's order. It opens with Guru Ram Das, and one of his first lines is worth carrying, in paraphrase: the Lord knows everything that happens inside a person, and lets not even a sesame seed's worth of anyone's effort go to waste. Second, the Bhagats. That's the Sikh name for the devotional poets, not Gurus themselves, whose hymns the Gurus set beside their own in the Granth. Gond makes room for them. Kabir the weaver is here, and Namdev, and Ravidas. Third, two of their voices. Namdev, in paraphrase: great sacrifices, giving away your weight in gold, bathing at the holy river meeting at Prayag, none of these equals singing the Lord's praise. Ravidas, in paraphrase: Mukand, Mukand, the Liberator; chant that name, world, for without the Liberator the body comes to nothing. Notice that neither one argues for his own importance. They point past themselves, and past every ceremony, to the Name. Fourth, why it matters that they're here. A scripture is a list of who gets heard. The Gurus could have kept their book to their own line. Instead, they made room for a weaver and a leatherworker, and Gond is one of the places you hear them. Guru Ram Das's opening line reads differently after you meet the Bhagats: not a sesame seed of anyone's effort wasted. Not a sesame seed of a weaver's, either. That's today's line: the bhagats' raga.
screen: `NOT A SESAME SEED OF EFFORT WASTED.` · `THE BHAGATS: KABIR, NAMDEV, RAVIDAS.` · `NOTHING EQUALS SINGING THE LORD'S PRAISE.` · `A SCRIPTURE IS A LIST OF WHO GETS HEARD.` · then, large: `THE BHAGATS' RAGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Gond, or listen for someone usually unheard. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Gond; a Bhagat's hymn is a good one to find. If not, sit and let your breathing ease. Bring to mind someone whose work you rely on and rarely notice: the person who cleans the building, drives the bus, picks the fruit, answers the phone. Hold their face, or imagine one. Let their effort count, not one sesame seed of it wasted. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for them. If you don't, simply keep them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Raga Gond. The raga after Bilaval, opened by Guru Ram Das, where Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas sing beside the Gurus. Today's word.
Your line: the bhagats' raga. Today, thank one person whose work you usually walk past, by name if you can, and let it be more than a nod. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Hymns of the Bhagats, such as Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas, are sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns, and Sikhs bow to the whole Granth, Bhagat bani included, as the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scripture is written by its founders.
what it means: the Granth sets devotional poets from humble trades beside the Gurus, and Gond makes room for them.
what a scholar hears: Gond (from ang 859) opens with Guru Ram Das and then carries Bhagat bani of Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas, beside the Gurus' hymns.

notes: Paraphrase of Gond Mahalla 4, Ang 859 (je man chit aas rakheh har oopar...; har jaanai sabh kichh jo jee vartai prabh ghaaliaa kisai kaa ik til na gavaaee). Please confirm the 'sesame seed' line is in the opening hymn.

Paraphrase of Namdev, Gond, Ang 873 (asumedh jagne, tulaa purakh daane, praag isnaane, tau na pujeh har keerat naamaa) and Ravidas, Gond, Ang 875 (mukand mukand japahu sansaar, bin mukand tan hoe aauhaar). Please confirm Angs and wording.

'Each of them names his own trade in his songs': Kabir (julaha), Namdev (chhimba, cloth printer) and Ravidas (chamar, leatherworker) do so in their hymns in the Granth, though not necessarily in Gond. Please confirm.
'In the towns they lived in, the people with titles and temple keys would not have sat them at the front' is a general framing of caste exclusion; confirm tone.
Original: ਗੋਂਡ; please confirm spelling (the heading is Raag Gond / Gaund).
